newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. ends Mideast mission with peace in balance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ends Mideast mission with peace in balance.

text.p: The United States ended its emergency Middle East mission waiting to see whether it had rescued Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking from collapsing under the impact of a suicide bombing against Israel.

U.S. Middle East troubleshooter Dennis Ross said he was heading home after four days to report on Thursday to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who promised to make her maiden visit to the region "in the coming days or weeks".

Ross told reporters after meeting Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat in the self-ruled West Bank town of Ramallah his mission had succeeded in restoring security contacts between the Palestinians and Israel, ruptured by the July 30 bombing of an Jerusalem market which killed 16 including the two bombers.

Ross shuttled between Arafat and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu and managed to bring Israeli and Palestinian security officials together to share intelligence. But the Americans said it was only a beginning.

"We consider it essential that the violence be stopped and everything be done by Chairman Arafat to make sure that the infrastructure of the terrorist groups is dismantled and that he make a 100 percent effort in order to make sure that the terrorist activities do not take place," Albright said.

She told reporters in Washington: "I want to wait to see exactly what these talks bring in terms of developing a better climate in terms of the security there. What we have to do is see actions, results."
Albright had said earlier she would make her first visit to the Middle East provided there was progress in security coordination.

Ross said he believed some of the punitive sanctions which Israel had imposed on Palestinians following the suicide attack, particularly the sealing off of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, would be eased. He did not say when this might happen.

"A measure that is clearly not directly related to security is not going to help the situation," Ross told CNN television. Asked for an example, Ross said: "Money", an apparent reference to tax funds collected from Palestinians by Israel and held up by Netanyahu because of the attack.
But Palestinian cabinet minister Nabil Shaath said Ross had failed in his meeting with Arafat to report any plans by Netanyahu to ease the sanctions on Palestinians.
"Ross came tonight with almost nothing from Mr Netanyahu," Shaath told a Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) function in Ramallah.

On a visit to Jordan, the Israeli prime minister had insisted Arafat would have to crack down on Islamic militants bent on making guerrilla attacks against the Jewish state before Israel would ease sanctions.
Arafat has insisted he is making a "100 percent effort" on security and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to undermine his legitimacy.
Senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters people should not be too optimistic about Ross's visit.

"We all knew that Mr Ross came at a time when the relations between us and Israel deteriorated to levels unprecedented," he said. "Madame Albright can, if she decides to put her weight, full weight (behind it)...save the process from collapsing."

Talks on expanding Palestinian self-rule set out in a 1993 interim peace accord with Israel have been been dormant since March when Netanyahu's government allowed construction to begin on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
